title: Bands at boxing, fireworks, churches and races
summary: They discuss whether bands played at boxing matches and racing; Kmen notes bands at fireworks, dances and church services.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Caldwell also was involved in promoting boxing, you know, the early theater, James Paul was. I wonder if they had any bands at boxing matches in it. Have you come across that?

I don't know. I haven't come across any such thing, and I've perused all the papers as closely as I can, but I'm not so sure, and I'm getting outside of anything I know much about, but I'm not so sure it was boxing. Very well known then, they might have had a boxer that they brought over or something like this, but Well they had them. I tend to think of boxing as post-Civil War.

Well I'll get in that class just spoke on the heavyweight championship and show if he was involved in some, I think a heavyweight championship match with an English rocker who he imported. I'll have to look it up.

He was a promoter all the way. He started the first Gasworks here, and he was in other business ventures, which went up and down, and the theater to him was another such venture, although I think his heart was always more in the theater. He'd started himself in an English company that he brought here in it was either 1817, I think it was 1817, and rented a little decrepit theater on St. Philip Street.

Well you hear about it later so much, playing between rounds is something I can't imagine happening today, but certainly within the memory of living people. I played between rounds. You played between rounds, right? Where?

In the military services. But that there of course is different. They had the bands, and the bands were always there to fight. Well there were a lot of occasions that were sporting where they had bands, and I just have never seen it in connection to boxing. But I don't know that you'd exactly call it a sport, but they were very fun in the fireworks exhibitions, and big blow-offs of fireworks, and you always have a band for these things in the country wherever they set up the firework exhibition. Or there might be a joint thing, a balloon ascension, and fireworks, and a band, always a band, and those things you can always find a band, a good musical monzique of some kind. It would be part of it, just an integral part of it. And then usually, the same band might turn to for dancing after the fireworks had gone off. It was very seldom that they had a band for any occasion, outside of a church service, that dancing didn't follow, and the band just converted to dancing. Of course they used the orchestras in the churches here, at least in the St. Louis Cathedral, and a custom that you don't see much of anymore, of playing for masses and playing for regular services. Sometimes as many as a 50-piece orchestra in the church.
What sort of racing did they have then? Horses and mules? Anything else?

I guess Dr. Hogan, I have to tell you more about that. I know there was a couple of clubs that got started very early here. One was called the Jockey Club or something like that, but I haven't followed. You haven't come across anything on bands? No, no, and in this respect, I can say I looked at it.
